expectedText:
BONUS AND INCENTIVE COMPENSATION AT TERMINATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Morgan T. Ellis · Acme Manufacturing, Inc.

DECLARATION AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Bonus and Incentive Compensation at Termination — Information Sheet is prepared with respect to Morgan T. Ellis's employment with Acme Manufacturing, Inc., which ended on March 14, 2026. It describes how California law treats bonus, incentive, and similar variable pay when employment ends — including the legal line California authorities draw between a bonus the employer retains discretion to pay or withhold, which is not itself a legally owed wage, and a bonus tied to an objective formula, quota, or other criteria the employee has already satisfied, which can be. This document addresses bonus and incentive compensation generally; it is separate from, and does not repeat, this project's Commission Payout Upon Termination document, which addresses commissions specifically — a form of pay tied to a written commission agreement governed by its own statute, Labor Code section 2751. The bonus or incentive arrangement addressed here is described as: Annual performance bonus, covering the period Calendar year 2025, under plan terms described as: 5% of base salary if annual sales quota met; must be employed on March 1 payment date.

"WAGES" IS A GENERAL DEFINITION — IT DOES NOT EXPRESSLY MENTION BONUSES
California's core statutory definition of "wages" is general: it covers "all amounts for labor performed by employees of every description," measured by the standard of time, task, piece, commission basis, "or other method of calculation" — a catch-all that does not, on its own text, use the word "bonus" or "incentive," or list bonus pay among its examples. Whether a bonus counts as a "wage" under this definition is instead something California's own labor enforcement agency has interpreted, not something the statute spells out for bonuses by name: the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's published glossary states that a bonus may be "a contractually required payment where a promise is made that a bonus will be paid in return for a specific result, such as exceeding a minimum sales figure or piece quota, or as an inducement to remain in the employ of the employer for a certain period of time," and that "[s]ums earned as bonuses are wages under the definition found in Labor Code Section 200." A bonus or incentive payment that Morgan T. Ellis contends was earned before March 14, 2026 is, on this interpretation, a "wage" reached by the same statutory protections that apply to wages generally — but only once, and to the extent, it was actually earned.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Wages” includes all amounts for labor performed by employees of every description, whether the amount is fixed or ascertained by the standard of time, task, piece, commission basis, or other method of calculation."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 200(a) (California Legislative Information text), the statutory definition of "wages" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=200.)
  "A bonus may be in the form of a gratuity where there is no promise for their payment, for example, a holiday bonus at the end of the year. Additionally, a bonus may be a contractually required payment where a promise is made that a bonus will be paid in return for a specific result, such as exceeding a minimum sales figure or piece quota, or as an inducement to remain in the employ of the employer for a certain period of time. Sums earned as bonuses are wages under the definition found in Labor Code Section 200."
  — California DLSE, Glossary of Terms — "bonus" (California Department of Industrial Relations text), DLSE Glossary, entry for "bonus" (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/Glossary.asp?Button1=B#bonus)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute and labor-agency interpretation, used as real evidence of how California treats bonus pay under its general wage definition — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific bonus arrangement, and not a claim that this same catch-all wording appears, or is interpreted the same way, in every other state's wage statute. The statutory text quoted below (Labor Code section 200(a)) was fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times; the DLSE glossary entry for "bonus" was fetched twice this session, directly from dir.ca.gov, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times. This clause and this document are informational only: this clause does not itself determine that any specific payment described in this document is a bonus, is a wage, or was actually earned before termination, and it does not determine that any specific amount is owed — that depends on the terms of the specific plan and the facts of the specific arrangement, addressed in this document's other clauses.

A GENUINELY DISCRETIONARY BONUS IS NOT, BY ITSELF, AN OWED WAGE
No section of the California Labor Code itself codifies a rule that a "discretionary" bonus is not a wage while a "nondiscretionary" bonus is. That specific vocabulary, and the line it draws, comes instead from the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's own sub-regulatory interpretation of the general wage statute, reflected in the agency's published Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual: "Bonuses which are completely discretionary, based on no objective criteria and are not routine, would not, of course, give rise to an implied bonus contract." On this interpretation, an employer's retained discretion over whether to pay a bonus at all, and how much to pay if it does, means no legal obligation to pay any particular amount has yet arisen — so there is nothing yet for a departing employee to have "earned" as a wage, unless and until the employer actually exercises that discretion in the employee's favor.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Discretionary Bonus. Bonuses which are completely discretionary, based on no objective criteria and are not routine, would not, of course, give rise to an implied bonus contract."
  — California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 35.4.3, "Discretionary Bonus" (June 2002; California Department of Industrial Relations text), DLSE Enforcement Manual § 35.4.3 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)
  Known gap: This is one state's labor-agency interpretation, used as real evidence that California's discretionary-bonus principle is agency guidance rather than codified statutory text — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific bonus arrangement. The quoted manual section comes from the DLSE's 2002 Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual (Section 35.4.3), fetched directly from dir.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical (by file checksum) across two fetches with different User-Agent headers; the same agency's own website states, on the page linking to this manual, that "[p]ursuant to Executive Order S-2-03, the DLSE opinion letters and the Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual are currently under review to determine their legal force and effect and to ensure compliance with the requirements of the Administrative Procedures Act" — meaning DLSE's own site flags this manual's binding legal weight as unresolved, and this particular section has not been revised since June 2002, so it does not reflect any California case law decided after that date. This research session's CourtListener case-law tools were rate-limited (125 requests/day, exhausted before this document's research began) and direct fetches to individual case pages on courtlistener.com, law.justia.com, and caselaw.findlaw.com were each blocked or returned no usable text when tested this session, so no case applying the discretionary-bonus principle directly, independent of the DLSE Manual's own description of it, was independently read this session; that gap is disclosed here rather than papered over. This clause and this document are informational only: this clause does not itself determine that any specific bonus or incentive arrangement described in this document is actually discretionary, nondiscretionary, or owed — that depends on the plan's own terms and the facts of the specific arrangement.

A BONUS TIED TO A QUOTA, FORMULA, OR OBJECTIVE CRITERIA CAN BECOME AN EARNED WAGE
Where a bonus is not left to the employer's unfettered discretion, but is instead promised in return for meeting an objective, ascertainable condition — a sales figure, a production quota, or simply remaining employed through a stated period, without the employer having reserved discretion over whether to pay it — California's labor enforcement agency has taken the position that the bonus can become earned by the employee's satisfaction of that condition, independent of any further discretionary act by the employer. The agency's Enforcement Manual illustrates this with a California Court of Appeal decision it describes as holding that, where a bonus was part of the inducement for continuing employment and the employer's plan did not expressly condition payment on continued employment through some later date, "the bonus is earned by the employee remaining in the employment of the employer." California's labor agency uses closely related language — "nondiscretionary bonus" — in a different but conceptually related context: computing the "regular rate of pay" used for overtime, where a bonus that compensates "for hours worked, production or proficiency, or as an incentive to remain employed by the same employer" must be folded into that calculation precisely because it is not discretionary.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "In Chinn v. China Nat. Aviation Corp. (1955) 138 Cal.App.2d 98, 291 P.2d 91 the court held that if the bonus is part of the inducement for the initial or continuing employment (see also Sabatini v. Hensley (1958) 161 Cal.App.2d 172, 326 P.2d 622; Hunter v. Ryan (1930) 109 Cal.App. 736, 293 P. 825) and where the employer, in announcing the plan, did not expressly qualify his promise to pay on any requirement of continued employment, the bonus is earned by the employee remaining in the employment of the employer."
  — California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 35.4.1, describing Chinn v. China Nat. Aviation Corp. (1955) 138 Cal.App.2d 98 (June 2002; California Department of Industrial Relations text), DLSE Enforcement Manual § 35.4.1 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)
  "A nondiscretionary bonus is included in determining the regular rate of pay for computing overtime when the bonus is compensation for hours worked, production or proficiency, or as an incentive to remain employed by the same employer."
  — California DLSE, "Overtime" FAQ (California Department of Industrial Relations text), DLSE FAQ - Overtime, Question 3 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/FAQ_Overtime.htm)
  Known gap: This is one state's labor-agency interpretation and case description, used as real evidence of California's approach to a formula- or quota-based bonus — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific bonus arrangement, and not a claim that any specific bonus described in this document actually meets this standard. The Chinn v. China Nat. Aviation Corp. (1955) 138 Cal.App.2d 98 discussion quoted below is reused as the DLSE Enforcement Manual (§ 35.4.1, June 2002) describes and quotes it, not independently verified against Chinn's own opinion text this session; this session's CourtListener access was rate-limited and direct fetches to case-law sites were blocked, as disclosed in this document's clause on discretionary bonuses, so that gap applies here as well and is not papered over. The DLSE "nondiscretionary bonus" language quoted below (from the agency's Overtime FAQ) is offered honestly for what it is: guidance developed for the different question of calculating the regular rate of pay for overtime, not guidance written specifically to answer whether a bonus must be paid out at termination — it is cited here only as further evidence that California's labor agency treats a formula- or quota-tied bonus as categorically different from a discretionary one, not as a holding about termination payout timing. This clause and this document are informational only: this clause does not itself determine that any specific bonus or incentive arrangement described in this document is actually nondiscretionary or owed — that depends on the plan's own terms and the facts of the specific arrangement.

A "MUST BE EMPLOYED ON THE PAYMENT DATE" CONDITION: ENFORCEABLE SOMETIMES, CONTESTED OFTEN
California authorities do not resolve, by a single clean rule, whether a bonus condition requiring the employee to still be employed on a future payment date is enforceable against an employee terminated before that date. The DLSE's Enforcement Manual describes the result as turning on how the condition was written: where the employer has "expressly qualified its promise of a bonus on a requirement of continued employment," an employee who leaves before the bonus calculation date is not entitled to receive it — a rule the manual traces to Lucien v. All States Trucking (1981) 116 Cal.App.3d 972, 975, and further back to Peterson v. California Shipbuilding Corp. (1947) 80 Cal.App.2d 827, 831. But where the bonus plan does not expressly condition payment on continued employment through that date, the same manual describes a different result: it discusses Hill v. Kaiser Aetna (1982) 130 Cal.App.3d 188, where an employee who resigned before a bonus's calculation date was nonetheless held to be vested in the prior year's bonus because the plan did not expressly require continued employment and the bonus itself was an inducement for continued employment. Which of these two lines of description applies to a specific bonus plan depends on the plan's own written terms — described here as: 5% of base salary if annual sales quota met; must be employed on March 1 payment date — and on whether March 14, 2026 fell before or after whatever date, if any, that plan specifies.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employee who voluntarily leaves his employment before the bonus calculation date is not entitled to receive it if the employer has expressly qualified its promise of a bonus on a requirement of continued employment. Lucien v. All States Trucking (1981) 116 Cal.App.3d 972, 975. This has been the rule ever since Peterson v. California Shipbuilding Corp. (1947) 80 Cal.App.2d 827, 831, 183 P.2d 56."
  — California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 35.2, describing Lucien v. All States Trucking (1981) 116 Cal.App.3d 972 and Peterson v. California Shipbuilding Corp. (1947) 80 Cal.App.2d 827 (June 2002; California Department of Industrial Relations text), DLSE Enforcement Manual § 35.2 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)
  "Where the promise of a bonus is not expressly conditioned on continued employment an employee who voluntarily leaves employment may be entitled to the bonus if other applicable conditions have been satisfied. Thus, in Hill v. Kaiser Aetna (1982) 130 Cal.App.3d 188, an employee who resigned on January 3, 1978, was held to be vested in his right to a bonus for calendar year 1977 where: (1) the bonus plan did not expressly require continued employment, and (2) the bonus was an inducement for continued employment."
  — California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 35.3, describing Hill v. Kaiser Aetna (1982) 130 Cal.App.3d 188 (June 2002; California Department of Industrial Relations text), DLSE Enforcement Manual § 35.3 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)
  Known gap: This is one state's labor-agency description of case law, used as real evidence that California's treatment of an employment-through-the-payment-date condition is fact- and plan-specific rather than resolved by one clean statutory rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific bonus plan, and not a claim about how any particular plan would actually be characterized. The two citations below are both drawn from the same document — Section 35 of the DLSE Enforcement Manual — describing two different cases with two different outcomes; they are presented here as one source's account of a split in outcomes, not as two independent corroborating sources for a single rule. The descriptions of Lucien v. All States Trucking, Peterson v. California Shipbuilding Corp., and Hill v. Kaiser Aetna are reused as the DLSE Enforcement Manual (§ 35.2-35.3, June 2002) describes them, not independently verified against each case's own opinion text this session; this session's CourtListener access was rate-limited and direct fetches to individual case pages were blocked, as disclosed in this document's clause on discretionary bonuses, and that same gap applies to all three cases named in this clause. This document set's Commission Payout Upon Termination document separately covers a related but distinct earned-versus-contingent distinction for commissions specifically, verified there against the commission case Steinhebel v. Los Angeles Times Communications, LLC directly; this clause does not repeat that verification because commissions and bonuses are governed by different lines of authority, as this document's declaration clause explains. This clause and this document are informational only: this clause does not itself determine that any specific bonus condition in any specific plan is enforceable or unenforceable, or that any specific amount is owed — that depends on the plan's own written terms and the facts of the specific arrangement.

EMPLOYER-INITIATED DISCHARGE BEFORE A BONUS PERIOD ENDS: A DIFFERENT QUESTION FROM A VOLUNTARY QUIT
The DLSE Enforcement Manual treats an employer-initiated discharge, before the terms of a bonus arrangement have been completed, as a legally different situation from an employee's own voluntary departure. Under common-law contract principles the manual applies, one party to a contract may not use its own act to prevent the other party from completing the conditions that would have entitled that party to performance: "If the employee is discharged before completion of all of the terms of the bonus agreement, and there is not valid cause, based on conduct of the employee, for the discharge, the employee may be entitled to recover at least a pro-rata share of the promised bonus." This is a distinct question from the discretionary-versus-nondiscretionary line addressed elsewhere in this document: it applies even to a bonus that would otherwise have required the employee to remain employed through a later date, where the reason employment did not continue was the employer's own decision to discharge the employee for reasons unrelated to the employee's conduct.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Termination Of The Employment By The Employer. Common law contract theories will not allow one party to the contract to prevent the other party from completing the contract. If the employee is discharged before completion of all of the terms of the bonus agreement, and there is not valid cause, based on conduct of the employee, for the discharge, the employee may be entitled to recover at least a pro-rata share of the promised bonus."
  — California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 35.4.4, "Termination Of The Employment By The Employer" (June 2002; California Department of Industrial Relations text), DLSE Enforcement Manual § 35.4.4 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)
  Known gap: This is one state's labor-agency interpretation of common-law contract principles, used as real evidence of how California's enforcement agency approaches a discharge-before-completion scenario for bonus pay — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific separation, and not a claim that any specific termination was, in fact, a discharge without cause as opposed to a voluntary quit or a discharge for cause. The quoted manual section (§ 35.4.4, June 2002) cites only an internal DLSE opinion letter (O.L. 1987.06.03) as its authority, not a published court decision; that opinion letter itself was not independently located or read this session, so this clause is disclosed as agency guidance describing a common-law contract principle, not as a case holding. This session's CourtListener case-law tools were rate-limited and direct case-page fetches were blocked, as disclosed in this document's clause on discretionary bonuses, and the same gap applies here: no independent published California decision squarely addressing pro-rata bonus recovery on a for-cause-less discharge was located and read this session. This clause and this document are informational only: this clause does not itself determine that any specific separation was, or was not, a discharge without cause, or that any specific pro-rata amount is owed — those are factual questions this clause does not resolve.

NOT EVERY BONUS-FORFEITURE CONDITION IS ENFORCEABLE — EVEN BEYOND THE DISCRETIONARY/NONDISCRETIONARY LINE
Even where a bonus plan expressly conditions payment on some fact about the employee's later status, California authorities have recognized that not every such condition will be enforced. The DLSE Enforcement Manual describes a California Court of Appeal decision striking down a bonus- and profit-sharing forfeiture condition that penalized an employee for going to work for a competitor after leaving, on the ground that the condition was "contrary to the strong public policy against contracts by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade or business" — the same public policy embodied in California's statute voiding most non-compete restrictions. This illustrates that the discretionary/nondiscretionary distinction addressed elsewhere in this document is not the only limit California law places on bonus-forfeiture conditions; a condition can be independently unenforceable for a reason unrelated to discretion, such as conflicting with a separate California public policy.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Illegal Conditions. Ware v. Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith, Inc. (1972) 24 Cal.App.3d 35, 100 Cal.Rptr. 791, involved a profit-sharing plan containing a provision that an employee who voluntarily terminated his employment and went to work for a competitor forfeited his rights to benefits under the plan. The court held that the forfeiture clause was invalid as it was contrary to the strong public policy against contracts by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade or business."
  — California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 35.4.2, describing Ware v. Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith, Inc. (1972) 24 Cal.App.3d 35 (June 2002; California Department of Industrial Relations text), DLSE Enforcement Manual § 35.4.2 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)
  Known gap: This is one state's labor-agency description of case law and a related statute, used as real evidence that a bonus-forfeiture condition can be independently unenforceable on grounds unrelated to the discretionary/nondiscretionary line — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific bonus plan, and not a claim that any particular condition in any particular plan is, or is not, enforceable. The Ware v. Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith, Inc. (1972) 24 Cal.App.3d 35 discussion quoted below is reused as the DLSE Enforcement Manual (§ 35.4.2, June 2002) describes it, not independently verified against the case's own opinion text this session, for the same CourtListener rate-limiting and blocked-direct-fetch reasons disclosed in this document's clause on discretionary bonuses. The underlying statute the manual cross-references, Business and Professions Code section 16600, is not itself independently fetched or quoted in this clause; it is named only as the manual names it, as the statutory embodiment of the public policy the described case applied. This clause and this document are informational only: this clause does not itself determine that any specific condition in any specific bonus plan is lawful or unlawful — that depends on the condition's own terms and the facts of the specific arrangement.

AN EARNED, UNPAID BONUS RIDES ON THE SAME FINAL-PAY DEADLINES AND WAITING-TIME PENALTY AS OTHER WAGES
Once a bonus or incentive payment is properly classified as an earned wage — as distinct from a still-discretionary or not-yet-earned amount — California law does not carve out a separate payment deadline or a separate penalty scheme for it. It is folded into the same final-wage-payment deadlines, and the same willful-nonpayment penalty, that apply to wages generally: where an employer willfully fails to pay wages due to a discharged or quitting employee, "the wages of the employee shall continue as a penalty from the due date thereof at the same rate until paid or until an action therefor is commenced," up to a cap of 30 days. Whether that penalty actually applies to a specific unpaid bonus depends on the same final-pay-timing and willfulness questions this project's Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document already addresses for unpaid wages generally.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "If an employer willfully fails to pay, without abatement or reduction, in accordance with Sections 201, 201.3, 201.5, 201.6, 201.8, 201.9, 202, and 205.5, any wages of an employee who is discharged or who quits, the wages of the employee shall continue as a penalty from the due date thereof at the same rate until paid or until an action therefor is commenced; but the wages shall not continue for more than 30 days."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 203(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=203.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that an earned bonus is folded into the same final-wage deadlines and waiting-time-penalty framework as other wages — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific separation, and not a claim that any specific bonus amount was actually earned, unpaid, or subject to a willful violation. This clause deliberately does not re-derive the specific final-pay deadlines of Labor Code sections 201 and 202, the full mechanics and 30-day cap of the waiting-time penalty, or the case law defining "willful" for this purpose, because this project's Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document already contains dedicated, separately verified clauses covering those in full; this clause exists only to connect an earned bonus, once recognized as a wage under this document's other clauses, to that already-covered framework rather than to duplicate it. The statutory text quoted below (Labor Code section 203(a)) was fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times, independently of that same section's earlier verification for this project's Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document — this is honestly the same statutory section already cited elsewhere in this corpus, re-verified rather than newly discovered, not a second independent source. This clause and this document are informational only: this clause does not itself determine that any specific bonus described in this document was actually earned, unpaid as of the termination date, or that the employer's failure to pay it, if any, was willful — those are factual and legal questions this clause does not resolve.

Period the bonus or incentive compensation covers: Calendar year 2025

expectedJSON.body: Where a bonus is not left to the employer's unfettered discretion, but is instead promised in return for meeting an objective, ascertainable condition — a sales figure, a production quota, or simply remaining employed through a stated period, without the employer having reserved discretion over whether to pay it — California's labor enforcement agency has taken the position that the bonus can become earned by the employee's satisfaction of that condition, independent of any further discretionary act by the employer. The agency's Enforcement Manual illustrates this with a California Court of Appeal decision it describes as holding that, where a bonus was part of the inducement for continuing employment and the employer's plan did not expressly condition payment on continued employment through some later date, "the bonus is earned by the employee remaining in the employment of the employer." California's labor agency uses closely related language — "nondiscretionary bonus" — in a different but conceptually related context: computing the "regular rate of pay" used for overtime, where a bonus that compensates "for hours worked, production or proficiency, or as an incentive to remain employed by the same employer" must be folded into that calculation precisely because it is not discretionary.

citations.case: California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 35.4.1, describing Chinn v. China Nat. Aviation Corp. (1955) 138 Cal.App.2d 98 (June 2002; California Department of Industrial Relations text)
citations.quote: In Chinn v. China Nat. Aviation Corp. (1955) 138 Cal.App.2d 98, 291 P.2d 91 the court held that if the bonus is part of the inducement for the initial or continuing employment (see also Sabatini v. Hensley (1958) 161 Cal.App.2d 172, 326 P.2d 622; Hunter v. Ryan (1930) 109 Cal.App. 736, 293 P. 825) and where the employer, in announcing the plan, did not expressly qualify his promise to pay on any requirement of continued employment, the bonus is earned by the employee remaining in the employment of the employer.

citations.case: California DLSE, "Overtime" FAQ (California Department of Industrial Relations text)
citations.quote: A nondiscretionary bonus is included in determining the regular rate of pay for computing overtime when the bonus is compensation for hours worked, production or proficiency, or as an incentive to remain employed by the same employer.

The Chinn v. China Nat. Aviation Corp. (1955) 138 Cal.App.2d 98 discussion quoted below is reused as the DLSE Enforcement Manual (§ 35.4.1, June 2002) describes and quotes it, not independently verified against Chinn's own opinion text this session; this session's CourtListener access was rate-limited and direct fetches to case-law sites were blocked, as disclosed in this document's clause on discretionary bonuses, so that gap applies here as well and is not papered over. The DLSE "nondiscretionary bonus" language quoted below (from the agency's Overtime FAQ) is offered honestly for what it is: guidance developed for the different question of calculating the regular rate of pay for overtime, not guidance written specifically to answer whether a bonus must be paid out at termination — it is cited here only as further evidence that California's labor agency treats a formula- or quota-tied bonus as categorically different from a discretionary one, not as a holding about termination payout timing. This clause and this document are informational only: this clause does not itself determine that any specific bonus or incentive arrangement described in this document is actually nondiscretionary or owed — that depends on the plan's own terms and the facts of the specific arrangement.

expectedJSON.body: California authorities do not resolve, by a single clean rule, whether a bonus condition requiring the employee to still be employed on a future payment date is enforceable against an employee terminated before that date. The DLSE's Enforcement Manual describes the result as turning on how the condition was written: where the employer has "expressly qualified its promise of a bonus on a requirement of continued employment," an employee who leaves before the bonus calculation date is not entitled to receive it — a rule the manual traces to Lucien v. All States Trucking (1981) 116 Cal.App.3d 972, 975, and further back to Peterson v. California Shipbuilding Corp. (1947) 80 Cal.App.2d 827, 831. But where the bonus plan does not expressly condition payment on continued employment through that date, the same manual describes a different result: it discusses Hill v. Kaiser Aetna (1982) 130 Cal.App.3d 188, where an employee who resigned before a bonus's calculation date was nonetheless held to be vested in the prior year's bonus because the plan did not expressly require continued employment and the bonus itself was an inducement for continued employment. Which of these two lines of description applies to a specific bonus plan depends on the plan's own written terms — described here as: 5% of base salary if annual sales quota met; must be employed on March 1 payment date — and on whether March 14, 2026 fell before or after whatever date, if any, that plan specifies.

citations.case: California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 35.2, describing Lucien v. All States Trucking (1981) 116 Cal.App.3d 972 and Peterson v. California Shipbuilding Corp. (1947) 80 Cal.App.2d 827 (June 2002; California Department of Industrial Relations text)
citations.quote: An employee who voluntarily leaves his employment before the bonus calculation date is not entitled to receive it if the employer has expressly qualified its promise of a bonus on a requirement of continued employment. Lucien v. All States Trucking (1981) 116 Cal.App.3d 972, 975. This has been the rule ever since Peterson v. California Shipbuilding Corp. (1947) 80 Cal.App.2d 827, 831, 183 P.2d 56.

citations.case: California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 35.3, describing Hill v. Kaiser Aetna (1982) 130 Cal.App.3d 188 (June 2002; California Department of Industrial Relations text)
citations.quote: Where the promise of a bonus is not expressly conditioned on continued employment an employee who voluntarily leaves employment may be entitled to the bonus if other applicable conditions have been satisfied. Thus, in Hill v. Kaiser Aetna (1982) 130 Cal.App.3d 188, an employee who resigned on January 3, 1978, was held to be vested in his right to a bonus for calendar year 1977 where: (1) the bonus plan did not expressly require continued employment, and (2) the bonus was an inducement for continued employment.

The two citations below are both drawn from the same document — Section 35 of the DLSE Enforcement Manual — describing two different cases with two different outcomes; they are presented here as one source's account of a split in outcomes, not as two independent corroborating sources for a single rule. The descriptions of Lucien v. All States Trucking, Peterson v. California Shipbuilding Corp., and Hill v. Kaiser Aetna are reused as the DLSE Enforcement Manual (§ 35.2-35.3, June 2002) describes them, not independently verified against each case's own opinion text this session; this session's CourtListener access was rate-limited and direct fetches to individual case pages were blocked, as disclosed in this document's clause on discretionary bonuses, and that same gap applies to all three cases named in this clause. This document set's Commission Payout Upon Termination document separately covers a related but distinct earned-versus-contingent distinction for commissions specifically, verified there against the commission case Steinhebel v. Los Angeles Times Communications, LLC directly; this clause does not repeat that verification because commissions and bonuses are governed by different lines of authority, as this document's declaration clause explains. This clause and this document are informational only: this clause does not itself determine that any specific bonus condition in any specific plan is enforceable or unenforceable, or that any specific amount is owed — that depends on the plan's own written terms and the facts of the specific arrangement.

expectedJSON.body: The DLSE Enforcement Manual treats an employer-initiated discharge, before the terms of a bonus arrangement have been completed, as a legally different situation from an employee's own voluntary departure. Under common-law contract principles the manual applies, one party to a contract may not use its own act to prevent the other party from completing the conditions that would have entitled that party to performance: "If the employee is discharged before completion of all of the terms of the bonus agreement, and there is not valid cause, based on conduct of the employee, for the discharge, the employee may be entitled to recover at least a pro-rata share of the promised bonus." This is a distinct question from the discretionary-versus-nondiscretionary line addressed elsewhere in this document: it applies even to a bonus that would otherwise have required the employee to remain employed through a later date, where the reason employment did not continue was the employer's own decision to discharge the employee for reasons unrelated to the employee's conduct.

citations.case: California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 35.4.4, "Termination Of The Employment By The Employer" (June 2002; California Department of Industrial Relations text)
citations.quote: Termination Of The Employment By The Employer. Common law contract theories will not allow one party to the contract to prevent the other party from completing the contract. If the employee is discharged before completion of all of the terms of the bonus agreement, and there is not valid cause, based on conduct of the employee, for the discharge, the employee may be entitled to recover at least a pro-rata share of the promised bonus.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's labor-agency interpretation of common-law contract principles, used as real evidence of how California's enforcement agency approaches a discharge-before-completion scenario for bonus pay — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific separation, and not a claim that any specific termination was, in fact, a discharge without cause as opposed to a voluntary quit or a discharge for cause. The quoted manual section (§ 35.4.4, June 2002) cites only an internal DLSE opinion letter (O.L. 1987.06.03) as its authority, not a published court decision; that opinion letter itself was not independently located or read this session, so this clause is disclosed as agency guidance describing a common-law contract principle, not as a case holding. This session's CourtListener case-law tools were rate-limited and direct case-page fetches were blocked, as disclosed in this document's clause on discretionary bonuses, and the same gap applies here: no independent published California decision squarely addressing pro-rata bonus recovery on a for-cause-less discharge was located and read this session. This clause and this document are informational only: this clause does not itself determine that any specific separation was, or was not, a discharge without cause, or that any specific pro-rata amount is owed — those are factual questions this clause does not resolve.

expectedJSON.body: Even where a bonus plan expressly conditions payment on some fact about the employee's later status, California authorities have recognized that not every such condition will be enforced. The DLSE Enforcement Manual describes a California Court of Appeal decision striking down a bonus- and profit-sharing forfeiture condition that penalized an employee for going to work for a competitor after leaving, on the ground that the condition was "contrary to the strong public policy against contracts by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade or business" — the same public policy embodied in California's statute voiding most non-compete restrictions. This illustrates that the discretionary/nondiscretionary distinction addressed elsewhere in this document is not the only limit California law places on bonus-forfeiture conditions; a condition can be independently unenforceable for a reason unrelated to discretion, such as conflicting with a separate California public policy.

citations.case: California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 35.4.2, describing Ware v. Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith, Inc. (1972) 24 Cal.App.3d 35 (June 2002; California Department of Industrial Relations text)
citations.quote: Illegal Conditions. Ware v. Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith, Inc. (1972) 24 Cal.App.3d 35, 100 Cal.Rptr. 791, involved a profit-sharing plan containing a provision that an employee who voluntarily terminated his employment and went to work for a competitor forfeited his rights to benefits under the plan. The court held that the forfeiture clause was invalid as it was contrary to the strong public policy against contracts by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade or business.

The Ware v. Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith, Inc. (1972) 24 Cal.App.3d 35 discussion quoted below is reused as the DLSE Enforcement Manual (§ 35.4.2, June 2002) describes it, not independently verified against the case's own opinion text this session, for the same CourtListener rate-limiting and blocked-direct-fetch reasons disclosed in this document's clause on discretionary bonuses. The underlying statute the manual cross-references, Business and Professions Code section 16600, is not itself independently fetched or quoted in this clause; it is named only as the manual names it, as the statutory embodiment of the public policy the described case applied. This clause and this document are informational only: this clause does not itself determine that any specific condition in any specific bonus plan is lawful or unlawful — that depends on the condition's own terms and the facts of the specific arrangement.

expectedJSON.body: Once a bonus or incentive payment is properly classified as an earned wage — as distinct from a still-discretionary or not-yet-earned amount — California law does not carve out a separate payment deadline or a separate penalty scheme for it. It is folded into the same final-wage-payment deadlines, and the same willful-nonpayment penalty, that apply to wages generally: where an employer willfully fails to pay wages due to a discharged or quitting employee, "the wages of the employee shall continue as a penalty from the due date thereof at the same rate until paid or until an action therefor is commenced," up to a cap of 30 days. Whether that penalty actually applies to a specific unpaid bonus depends on the same final-pay-timing and willfulness questions this project's Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document already addresses for unpaid wages generally.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 203(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If an employer willfully fails to pay, without abatement or reduction, in accordance with Sections 201, 201.3, 201.5, 201.6, 201.8, 201.9, 202, and 205.5, any wages of an employee who is discharged or who quits, the wages of the employee shall continue as a penalty from the due date thereof at the same rate until paid or until an action therefor is commenced; but the wages shall not continue for more than 30 days.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that an earned bonus is folded into the same final-wage deadlines and waiting-time-penalty framework as other wages — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific separation, and not a claim that any specific bonus amount was actually earned, unpaid, or subject to a willful violation. This clause deliberately does not re-derive the specific final-pay deadlines of Labor Code sections 201 and 202, the full mechanics and 30-day cap of the waiting-time penalty, or the case law defining "willful" for this purpose, because this project's Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document already contains dedicated, separately verified clauses covering those in full; this clause exists only to connect an earned bonus, once recognized as a wage under this document's other clauses, to that already-covered framework rather than to duplicate it.
